quests.scene: A friend asks how her wedding speech went. The story about her grandfather was moving, but the ending felt rushed.
options: It was pretty good, though you talked a bit fast.
Your speech was fine, but the ending was weak and I think people noticed it.
Great job! Everyone loved it, especially the ending, so no changes needed.
The story about your grandfather really moved people. The ending felt rushed, though — maybe slow down there?
quests.hint: Name one specific strength and one specific fix.
quests.explanation: Praising a specific moment and pointing to one fixable part makes the feedback believable and useful. Vague praise or blanket criticism gives her nothing to act on.
quests.culturalNote: Specific feedback is easier to trust than general compliments.

quests.instruction: Pick the best feedback to give.
quests.scene: A junior colleague has sent you a report with several number errors, and you want to help without discouraging him.
options: The report has a lot of problems, so I've marked them all for you to correct before tomorrow morning.
It's not ready to send to the client yet, so please go through it again and see what you find.
Thanks, I'll fix the numbers myself this afternoon.
There's good content here. Let's fix the numbers together.
quests.hint: Balance honesty with support and a shared next step.
quests.explanation: A short positive note plus a joint fix keeps morale up and solves the problem. Marking errors alone, sending him back blind, or fixing it silently teach little.
quests.culturalNote: Junior staff learn faster when feedback comes with a way to improve.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: Your manager tells you that you often interrupt others in meetings. You hadn't noticed.
options: Thanks for telling me. Could you point out an example so I can watch for it?
I don't think I interrupt that often, but I'll keep it in mind from now on.
Others interrupt more than I do, so it seems unfair to single me out for it.
You're right, I'm terrible at listening, and I always have been, ever since school.
quests.hint: Accept the feedback and ask for something concrete.
quests.explanation: Thanking her and asking for an example turns vague feedback into something you can change. Denial, deflection, or harsh self-criticism block progress.
quests.culturalNote: Asking for an example shows openness and helps you act on feedback.

quests.scene: A friend shares a health claim online that you know has been disproved. You want to disagree without embarrassing him.
options: That's not true, and you shouldn't share it, since it could mislead people.
I read something different — that study was disproved. Want me to send you the article so we can look together?
Maybe, I'm not sure, I'll have to think about that some more later on.
Everyone knows that's a myth, so I'm surprised you would believe it at all.
quests.hint: Offer evidence and a joint look.
quests.explanation: Offering a source to check together respects his intelligence. Direct commands, vague doubt, or ridicule turn it into a contest.
quests.culturalNote: Sharing sources tends to invite curiosity rather than defensiveness.

quests.scene: In a meeting, a senior executive presents a projection you think is too optimistic.
options: That's not what the data shows, so I think we should reconsider the whole plan.
I see it slightly differently. Could I share the numbers that led me there?
You're the expert here, so I'm sure your view is right and mine is probably wrong.
I disagree, but I'll do what you decide.
quests.hint: Disagree by offering evidence, not opposition.
quests.explanation: Framing your view as a different reading and offering data is respectful and constructive. Blunt contradiction or silent deference doesn't inform the decision.
quests.culturalNote: Disagreeing with senior people usually lands better when grounded in data.

quests.scene: Dinner with the family turns heated when politics come up.
options: You always get like this when we talk about politics, and it ruins every family dinner we have.
I don't want to argue at dinner, so I'll just stay quiet and not say anything more about it.
Let's agree to disagree and pass the potatoes.
Maybe we should discuss something else, since some of us have very different opinions here.
quests.hint: Close the argument lightly without winning it.
quests.explanation: A light, friendly close ends the argument without blame. Accusations or withdrawing leave tension in the room.
quests.culturalNote: Humor is a common way to defuse family arguments, though it depends on the family.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: At a party, friends push you to have a drink, but you're driving and don't want one.
options: No thanks, I don't drink, and I'd appreciate it if people stopped asking me about it.
Okay, just one, then, but I won't have any more, I promise you all.
Drinking's really not my thing, and I think it's silly that everybody's making a big deal of it.
I'm good with this, thanks — I'm driving. Who's up for a game?
quests.hint: Decline once, give a simple reason, and change the subject.
quests.explanation: A calm no with a reason and a new topic moves things on. Lecturing, giving in, or criticizing others prolongs the pressure.
quests.culturalNote: Offering an alternative activity is a common way to redirect social pressure.

quests.scene: Coworkers start gossiping about your boss at a Friday lunch and ask you to join in.
options: I don't really have anything to say about the boss, and I'd rather not get involved in the gossip.
I've heard things too, but I shouldn't say.
I'd rather not talk about him behind his back.
Let's not talk about work, since it's the weekend and we're supposed to be relaxing.
quests.hint: State your limit plainly without judging them.
quests.explanation: A short, calm limit avoids lecturing. Long explanations, hints, or deflections either invite more pressure or share what you shouldn't.
quests.culturalNote: Refusing to gossip is usually respected, especially when stated without judgment.

quests.scene: A close friend asks you to lend him money for the third time. You don't want to mix money and friendship.
options: I care about you, but I don't lend money to friends — it's a rule that protects the friendship. I can help you look at options.
I'd love to help you out, but I'm a bit short myself at the moment, so I can't.
I can lend you fifty, but I really need it back by Friday, no matter what happens.
You should ask your family for the money, because I don't think it's my place.
quests.hint: Set a principle, not an excuse, and offer another kind of help.
quests.explanation: Stating a personal rule and offering other help is honest and caring. Excuses, conditional loans, or redirecting can strain trust.
quests.culturalNote: Personal rules about lending money are common and easier to accept than invented excuses.

quests.scene: A colleague proudly tells you his new salary, which is well above yours, and asks what you make.
options: That's nice for you, but I don't think it's appropriate to talk about pay at work.
Wow, that's a lot more than I earn, and I guess I should have negotiated harder.
Good for you. I suppose some people are just luckier than others in this company.
Congratulations. I'd rather not compare numbers, but I'm glad it's going well for you.
quests.hint: Be warm, and keep your boundary.
quests.explanation: Congratulating him while declining to compare respects both of you. Lecturing, revealing your pay, or sniping changes the tone.
quests.culturalNote: Attitudes toward sharing salary vary; declining politely is always acceptable.

quests.scene: A friend criticizes your partner and you're not comfortable with it.
options: You don't know him the way I do, so I don't think you should be judging him so quickly.
I hear your concern, but I'd rather not discuss him like that.
Maybe you're right, I've wondered about that too.
Everyone has flaws, including your partner, so let's not start pointing fingers at each other.
quests.hint: Acknowledge her worry and set a limit.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging her care while ending the topic protects the relationship. Defensiveness, agreement, or counter-accusations escalate.
quests.culturalNote: Close friends often criticize out of concern, so acknowledging the intent helps.

quests.scene: A friend proudly shows you a very expensive purchase and asks what you think. You'd have chosen differently.
options: I think you paid too much for it, and there are better options available for less.
It looks well made. What made you pick it over the other one?
It's nice, I suppose, if you like that sort of thing, though it isn't really my taste.
Wow, amazing! You must be so happy, and I'm so jealous of you right now.
quests.hint: Find something true and ask a curious question.
quests.explanation: A true compliment and a real question stay honest and friendly. Blunt criticism, faint praise, or fake envy either hurt or mislead.
quests.culturalNote: Curious questions let you engage without lying or criticizing.

quests.scene: A client says your design 'just doesn't feel right' but can't say why.
options: Thanks — could you tell me what feels off? I'd like to get it right.
I followed the brief exactly, so I'm not sure what else you expected me to do here.
I'm sorry you don't like it, but a lot of other clients have loved this style.
I'll change it, but you should have told me what you wanted at the start of the project.
quests.hint: Ask for specifics without defending.
quests.explanation: A short, open question moves the client from feelings to details. Defending, comparing, or blaming closes the door.
quests.culturalNote: Vague feedback often improves once you ask what specifically feels wrong.

quests.scene: A friend says, 'You talk about yourself a lot.' It stings, but she has a point.
options: I don't think that's true, because I ask people about themselves quite a lot already.
You're right, I'm a terrible friend, and I'm sorry I've been so selfish all these years.
Thanks for the feedback, though I'd say you do exactly the same thing to me sometimes.
That's hard to hear, but I appreciate you being honest. Can you give me an example, so I can pay attention to it?
quests.hint: Acknowledge the sting and ask for something usable.
quests.explanation: Naming the discomfort while asking for an example shows openness. Denying, over-apologizing, or counter-attacking avoid the feedback.
quests.culturalNote: Hard feedback from friends can be a sign of trust.

quests.scene: A peer publicly criticizes your project plan in a meeting, and you think part of it is unfair.
options: Thanks for raising that. I'd like to look into it and follow up after the meeting.
That's not a fair criticism, and I think you're misunderstanding the whole project entirely.
You should have brought this up with me privately, instead of doing it in front of everyone.
You're right, I made a mistake, and I feel terrible about it in front of everyone here.
quests.hint: Stay calm and move it offline.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging and deferring avoids a public fight and protects the project. Rebuttal, scolding, or self-blame all escalate.
quests.culturalNote: In many workplaces, taking heated topics offline is a sign of professionalism.

quests.scene: Your friends want to skip class for the afternoon. You'd rather go.
options: You guys go ahead, because I don't want to get in trouble for skipping, and I've already missed too many.
I'm going to class — catch you at lunch?
I don't think it's a good idea to skip, since we have a test soon and could really use the notes.
Maybe I'll come if I can leave early.
quests.hint: Say what you're doing and keep the friendship.
quests.explanation: A short statement plus a plan to meet keeps things friendly. Explanations, lectures, or maybes give more room for pressure.
quests.culturalNote: Short, casual refusals often work best with peers.

quests.scene: Your team agrees on a timeline you think is too tight, and everyone seems ready to move on.
options: I don't think we should do this, and I'm surprised none of you can see how risky it is.
If everyone's happy with it, then I'm sure it's fine, and I won't say anything about my doubts.
Before we finalize, can I play devil's advocate on the timeline? I'm worried it's too tight.
I have a few concerns, but they're probably unimportant, so maybe we could discuss them later, if ever.
quests.hint: Raise the concern before the decision closes.
quests.explanation: Framing your worry as a test of the plan makes it easier to hear. Blunt opposition, silence, or downplaying leave the risk unaddressed.
quests.culturalNote: 'Devil's advocate' is a familiar way to invite challenge without personal conflict.

quests.scene: A cousin urges you to invest in a scheme that promises high returns and seems unclear.
options: Thanks for thinking of me, but I don't invest in anything I can't check independently. I'll pass, and I'd suggest you look into it carefully too.
That sounds like a scam, and I really think you should stay away from it altogether.
I'm not sure I've got enough money, but it sounds interesting, so send me the details.
I'll think about it, but I need to talk to my partner first, so I can't promise anything.
quests.hint: Decline on principle and express care.
quests.explanation: Stating your rule and caring for him keeps the family relationship while protecting you. Accusing, hedging, or stalling don't help either of you.
quests.culturalNote: Family investment pitches are common; a personal rule is easy to accept.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: Someone posts an offensive joke in a group chat and a few people react with laughing emojis.
options: Can we keep the jokes in this chat a bit more respectful, please, since some of us feel uncomfortable?
I'm sure you didn't mean it, but I think some people might find that joke hurtful.
Ha ha, very funny, maybe next time try a different type of joke, if you don't mind.
That joke isn't okay with me.
quests.hint: State your own view briefly.
quests.explanation: A short, personal statement is hard to argue with and makes your limit clear. Group-speaking, excuses, or fake laughter dilute it.
quests.culturalNote: Speaking for yourself avoids claiming to represent people who haven't spoken.

quests.scene: Your friends never invite Ben, a quiet member of the group. You'd like to change that gently.
options: It's not fair that we never invite Ben, and it makes us look like a really mean group.
I'm sure Ben has other plans this time.
Should we invite Ben too? He'd probably like to come.
I'll invite him on my own, because you clearly don't want to include him in the plans.
quests.hint: Suggest it as a question, not a criticism.
quests.explanation: A simple question invites the group to agree without feeling accused. Accusations, avoidance, or ultimatums create resistance.
quests.culturalNote: Framing inclusion as a suggestion works better than criticism of the group.

quests.scene: Two of your friends have argued, and one asks you to say who's right.
options: I think you're both right in some ways, but it's really something you two should sort out.
I'd rather not get involved, because it's between the two of you and not my problem.
You're being unfair to her, and I think you should apologize before things get any worse.
I care about you both, so I don't want to take sides. I'm happy to listen if it helps, though.
quests.hint: Stay neutral and available.
quests.explanation: Declining to take sides while offering to listen keeps both friendships. Splitting the difference, avoiding, or judging can each cost you.
quests.culturalNote: Being asked to take sides is common; supportive neutrality is often the safest response.

quests.scene: You're telling a job candidate that they weren't selected.
options: We were impressed by your experience, but unfortunately we've chosen someone whose skills are a closer match to the role.
We've had a lot of applicants, so we can't offer you the position, but we wish you the best.
Thank you for your time. We've decided to go with another candidate.
Thanks for coming in. We'll keep your CV on file, and we might contact you if anything changes.
quests.hint: Be clear and kind without giving false hope.
quests.explanation: A short, courteous, clear message respects the candidate's time. Long justifications, generic replies, or vague hopes can mislead.
quests.culturalNote: Clear rejections are generally kinder than open-ended ones.

quests.scene: A teammate proposes an ambitious idea that would cost twice your budget.
options: That won't work, because the budget is too small, so let's drop it and think of something else.
I like the ambition. The budget is the sticking point — can we look at cheaper options?
It's a great idea, but maybe not right now, and possibly not this year, we'll see how it goes.
I love it, but I'm not the one who decides, so you should ask someone else about it.
quests.hint: Credit the idea and name the real obstacle.
quests.explanation: Naming a specific constraint and offering to problem-solve keeps the idea alive. Rejecting, delaying vaguely, or passing the buck doesn't help.
quests.culturalNote: Explaining why something won't work makes 'no' easier to accept.

quests.scene: A close friend asks you to be her bridesmaid, but work will prevent you from taking part in all the planning.
options: I'm sorry, I'd love to do it, but I just don't think the timing will be right for me.
I'll think about it and let you know, though I can't promise anything at this stage.
I'm honored you asked. I can't commit to a bridesmaid's role because of work, but I'd love to help in another way.
I'm not really a bridesmaid person, so I'd rather not do it, and I hope that's okay.
quests.hint: Thank her, be honest, and offer something else.
quests.explanation: Gratitude, honesty, and an alternative preserve the friendship. Vague timing, stalling, or a blunt refusal don't.
quests.culturalNote: Being asked to be part of a wedding party is meaningful, so a warm reply matters.

quests.scene: Someone comments online with an opinion you disagree with.
options: I respectfully disagree with your post, and I think there are several factual errors in your argument that need correcting.
That's a really uninformed opinion, and I'd suggest you do some more research before posting anything else.
I'm sorry you feel that way, but you're wrong.
I see it differently, but thanks for sharing your view.
quests.hint: Disagree without escalating.
quests.explanation: A short, polite note of difference keeps the conversation civil. Point-by-point corrections or insults invite arguments.
quests.culturalNote: Online disagreements often escalate; brevity can help.

quests.scene: A neighbor complains that your car blocks his view when you park on the street.
options: The rules say I can park there, and I don't think you have any right to complain.
I understand your concern. Would it help if I parked on the other side after six?
I'll try to park elsewhere, but it's difficult because there isn't much space on this street.
I've parked there for years, and nobody has ever complained about it before you did.
quests.hint: Acknowledge the concern and offer a workable change.
quests.explanation: Offering a specific compromise keeps things friendly. Citing rules, vague promises, or history defend your position but don't solve the issue.
quests.culturalNote: Local parking rules differ, and neighborly solutions are usually better than legal arguments.

quests.scene: In literature class, you interpret a passage differently from your teacher.
options: I don't agree with your interpretation, and I think the text supports a different reading.
That's an interesting view, but I'm not sure it's what the author meant in the passage.
I read that passage a bit differently. I saw the narrator as unreliable — could I explain why?
You may be right, and I'm probably wrong, so I'll just go with your interpretation.
quests.hint: Present your reading as a question, with reasons.
quests.explanation: Asking to explain your view invites discussion and shows critical thinking. Blunt disagreement or silent deferral doesn't.
quests.culturalNote: Many teachers welcome alternate interpretations backed by evidence.

quests.scene: Your boss gives you feedback in front of the team. You agree with one point but disagree with another.
options: Thanks. I agree on the timeline. I'd like to talk about the budget point separately if that's okay.
I don't think that's fair, and I'd like to respond to each of your points right now.
I understand your comments, and I'll make all the changes you asked for, right away.
Thank you for the feedback, though I think there may have been a misunderstanding on your part.
quests.hint: Accept what's valid and defer the rest.
quests.explanation: Agreeing where you can and moving the rest offline is calm and professional. Publicly rebutting, over-agreeing, or hinting at her mistake create problems.
quests.culturalNote: Splitting agreement from disagreement helps you keep credibility.

quests.scene: A friend keeps giving you advice when you're just trying to vent.
options: Thanks — I'm just venting right now, not looking for advice.
I appreciate that you care, but I'd rather make my own decisions and learn from my own mistakes.
I've heard all that before, and I know what I'm doing, so you don't need to keep telling me.
Thanks, I'll think about it if I have time.
quests.hint: Tell her what kind of support you want.
quests.explanation: Naming what you need lets her help in the right way. Lectures, irritation, or fake agreement don't fix the mismatch.
quests.culturalNote: Telling friends whether you want advice or just listening is a common, healthy habit.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: At work, colleagues expect everyone to stay late tonight. You can stay a little while but not indefinitely.
options: I'm sorry, I can't stay late tonight, since I have plans that I can't change at short notice.
Fine, I'll stay as long as it takes, but I'm not happy about it at all, so please remember that.
I can stay until six tonight, but I can't do later. Let's decide what's most important to finish by then.
Everyone should be allowed to leave at five, because working late isn't fair to anyone.
quests.hint: Set your limit and help the team prioritize.
quests.explanation: Stating a clear limit and offering to prioritize is cooperative. Refusing outright, resenting, or generalizing don't help the team.
quests.culturalNote: Overtime norms vary widely between workplaces and countries.
